findings.title: Hardcoded fallback API secret token in client binary for JIT SSH certificate signing
findings.description: The open_native_tunnel command uses a hardcoded fallback secret 'proxync_default_secret_2026' when PROXYNC_API_SECRET_TOKEN is not defined in environment variables. Because this code compiles into the distributed desktop executable, any user can extract this token and authenticate against the backend JIT signing endpoint.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. An attacker inspects strings within the compiled desktop executable.
2. The attacker extracts 'proxync_default_secret_2026'.
3. The attacker issues HTTP POST requests to https://api.proxync.dev/api/tunnel/sign-jit-cert with 'Authorization: Bearer proxync_default_secret_2026' and submits their own public SSH key for arbitrary target subdomains.
4. If the server trusts this secret without per-user auth, the attacker hijacks subdomains and intercepts traffic.
findings.impact: Potential unauthorized SSH key registration and subdomain takeover on proxync.dev.
findings.recommendation: Authenticate JIT certificate signing requests using the user's dynamic workspace session token or client OAuth token rather than a hardcoded static secret.

findings.title: Path traversal and unrestricted local file reading in read_file_content IPC command
findings.description: read_file_content joins root_path and rel_path using Path::join after only stripping leading slashes. Directory traversal sequences (../ or ..\) are preserved, allowing resolution outside the root directory.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. A caller passes rel_path with directory traversal sequences (e.g., '../../../../Windows/System32/drivers/etc/hosts' or '../../../.ssh/id_rsa').
2. The command reads the sensitive target file from disk and returns the raw string content across the IPC bus.
findings.impact: Arbitrary local file read and sensitive credential exposure on the host system.
findings.recommendation: Canonicalize both root_path and the combined path using std::fs::canonicalize() and verify that the target path begins with the canonical root directory before reading.

findings.title: Dynamic unpinned remote code execution via npx -y in tunnel spawners
findings.description: open_localtunnel and open_cloudflare_tunnel invoke 'npx -y localtunnel@2.0.2' and 'npx -y --package=cloudflared cloudflared tunnel' dynamically at runtime. 'npx -y' downloads and executes packages from npm without local lockfile verification or binary hash pinning.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. An attacker publishes a compromised version or typo-squatted package, or compromises upstream npm packages.
2. When a user starts a tunnel in the desktop app, npx automatically fetches and runs arbitrary executable code with the user's desktop privileges.
findings.impact: Arbitrary remote code execution on the user's host operating system.
findings.recommendation: Bundle pre-built, cryptographically verified sidecar binaries with the desktop installer rather than downloading packages dynamically via npx at runtime.

findings.title: Subdomain CLI flag injection risk in open_native_tunnel SSH command
findings.description: clean_subdomain filters characters to alphanumeric and hyphens, but allows leading hyphens (e.g. '-oProxyCommand=...'). When passed to the ssh command argument vector, an argument starting with '-' may be parsed as an option flag by the OpenSSH client.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. A user or configuration provides a subdomain starting with '-' followed by OpenSSH configuration directives.
2. The OpenSSH client interprets the argument as a flag rather than a positional tunnel parameter.
findings.impact: Unintended SSH option injection or command argument corruption.
findings.recommendation: Validate subdomains with a strict regex requiring leading and trailing alphanumeric characters (^[a-z0-9][a-z0-9-]{0,62}[a-z0-9]$).

findings.title: Exposure of Bearer token in process command line arguments via curl
findings.description: open_native_tunnel spawns an external 'curl' process and passes 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' in the command line argument list. Command line arguments are visible to all processes running in the user session via process inspection tools and event logs.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. Unprivileged software running in the same user session monitors process creation events (Windows Event ID 4688, Task Manager, Get-Process).
2. The bearer token is captured in cleartext from the curl argument list.
findings.impact: Local credential exposure to other applications and processes.
findings.recommendation: Replace external curl execution with native in-process HTTP requests using reqwest.

findings.title: Permissive default Windows file ACL fallback in open_native_tunnel
findings.description: When setting ACLs on the generated private SSH key using icacls, if the USERNAME environment variable is empty or unset, the command grants read permission to 'Everyone'.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. The application runs in an environment where USERNAME is unset.
2. icacls grants read access on the private key to 'Everyone', allowing any local user on the machine to read the generated SSH private key.
findings.impact: Insecure key permissions on multi-user Windows machines.
findings.recommendation: Query the current user token or SID directly, or fail securely if the user identity cannot be resolved.

findings.title: Unredacted request body logging and plaintext persistence on disk
findings.description: start_proxy masks sensitive headers like Authorization and Cookie, but captures and emits request body previews verbatim. Authentication payloads (passwords, tokens) are transmitted via IPC and saved unencrypted to data.json in AppData.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. A developer tests authentication routes (e.g. POST /login or POST /oauth/token) through Proxync.
2. Passwords and credentials in the request body are captured and stored in unencrypted plaintext on disk.
findings.impact: Credential leakage in log history and stored workspace state.
findings.recommendation: Apply pattern-based masking on request body previews for common credential field names before emitting and saving logs.

findings.title: Unpinned third-party GitHub Actions in release workflows with code-signing secrets
findings.description: GitHub Actions in release workflows are referenced by mutable tags (e.g. v1, v4, stable) rather than full commit SHAs. In release.yml, TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY is passed into tauri-apps/tauri-action@v1.
findings.exploit_scenario:
1. A third-party action repository tag is compromised or retagged.
2. The workflow executes the compromised action, exposing TAURI_SIGNING_PRIVATE_KEY or modifying release binaries during the build.
findings.impact: Supply chain compromise and code-signing key exfiltration.
findings.recommendation: Pin all GitHub Actions to full immutable 40-character commit SHAs with inline version comments.
